John Toshack on Bill Shankly, Liverpool and an extraordinary football career

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that bill Shankly knew how to make an instant impact on players.
  • It has been revealed that the Welshman has never forgotten Shankly’s first words to him.
  • Industry observers note that over the next eight years, Toshack’s religious experience would develop him from a highly promising forward into an Anfield legend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that bill Shankly knew how to make an instant impact on players. The year was 1970 and John Toshack had just joined Liverpool from Cardiff for a club-record £110,000 fee, when he was greeted by his new manager.

It has been revealed that the Welshman has never forgotten Shankly’s first words to him. “I was only 21 and didn’t have a driving licence, so I travelled from Cardiff by train,” Toshack recounts to FourFourTwo. “Bill Shankly was waiting for me at the station, with his trilby on his head. The first thing he remarked to me was, ‘Welcome to Liverpool, son: you’ve come out of school to come to church’.”.

Industry observers note that over the next eight years, Toshack’s religious experience would develop him from a highly promising forward into an Anfield legend. That day at Liverpool Lime Street station, his extraordinary life in football was just getting started.

Today, 55 years later, following a career that took him to a dozen countries, he lives in Besalu – a village of medieval architecture in Catalonia, not far from the French border – with his wife, Mai, and several dogs they’ve adopted. As a manager, Toshack had seven spells in Spain: three at Real Sociedad, two with Real Madrid, plus stints at Deportivo La Coruna and Real Murcia. He welcomes FFT into his rural home, telling us he used to read the magazine when he lived in the UK.

According to recent reports, time hasn’t eroded a single detail of his extensive career, right back to his school days in his home city of Cardiff. “I’d take my sandwich with me so I didn’t have to go home for lunch – it meant I could stay and play football in the playground,” explains Toshack with a smile. Not just football, either: “I played cricket during the week, rugby on Saturday mornings and football in the afternoon,” he adds.

Then the first scouts appeared. At 15, he received an offer from Tottenham to go to London for trials. “I went with two other team-mates to a residence next to the old White Hart Lane,” he recalls. “We trained, and I thought they were going to give me a chance. But when I returned home, I got a letter thanking me but saying they didn’t believe I was good enough. I was gutted.”.

According to recent reports, his father, George, was a carpenter; a self-made man from Scotland. Young John’s mother encouraged him not to drop out of school, wanting him to have an alternative if he didn’t achieve his ultimate goal of becoming a footballer. Toshack, however, soon began breaking barriers locally. His first-team debut for Cardiff came aged 16, against Leyton Orient. Back then, only one substitution was allowed per team. “I came on with 10 minutes to go and scored a goal,” he says. “I can still visualise it today, if I close my eyes. A week later, we travelled up north to Middlesbrough. I started and scored two goals in 20 minutes. We won 4-3. It was a dream start.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Recent findings suggest that making a name for himself in the Second Division, Toshack caught the eye of Fulham in 1968. “Bobby Robson came in with an offer of £60,000, which was good money at the time,” he says. “But I thought London was too significant for a boy from South Wales, and turned it down. The Cardiff management were outraged at my decision. The transfer would have been a big money-spinner for them.”.

It has been revealed that toshack would score exactly 100 goals for Cardiff, in 207 appearances. More approaches were inevitable. In 1970, one arrived from Liverpool, who were attempting to return to the summit of English football after title triumphs under Shankly in 1964 and 1966. Cardiff boss Jimmy Scoular lived down the road from Toshack, and delivered the news. “I saw him one Sunday morning and I knew he wanted to tell me something notable,” continues Toshack. “He had read the papers, and they said Liverpool were coming for me. Shankly had offered £110,000, which was a record amount. Jimmy told me that we couldn’t say no. I thought, ‘This time, I’m ready’. Besides, Liverpool wasn’t Fulham.”.

Anfield awaited. “There was a lot of expectation,” admits Toshack. “In those days, we barely warmed up – we’d come out five minutes before kick-off and you could hear You’ll Never Walk Alone. The noise was deafening.”.

Industry observers note that his debut was rushed: he had suffered a minor ankle injury in his last game for Cardiff, but media expectation and his own desire to pull on a Liverpool shirt won out. “The following week, after treatment, it was the Merseyside derby against Everton,” he indicates. “It couldn’t have been better. There were 54,000 supporters in the stands, 27,000 of them behind the Kop, all on their feet. I scored my first goal with a header from Steve Heighway’s cross, against Everton’s centre-back, Brian Labone. That’s when my love story with Liverpool began.”.

According to recent reports, playing at Anfield never ceased to be a thrill. “We liked to attack the goal at the Kop end in the second half, in front of all of those fans, but other clubs knew that and tried to win the toss to spite us,” says Toshack, chuckling. Not long after the 6ft 1in striker’s arrival, a fellow young forward called Kevin Keegan signed from Scunthorpe United. A famous partnership was born.

Sources indicate that “Shankly put us together in attack in training, and there was great chemistry between the two of us from the start,” claims Toshack. “Keegan would say to me, ‘Anywhere you like, Tosh’. I’d jump up with a smile on my face, as I knew that if I won the jump and touched the ball, he’d find it for a finish.

It has been revealed that “We understood each other so well that we were once invited onto a TV show to see if telepathy existed between us. They put our backs to each other and we had to guess the colour or the number of a paddle that the other one held up. I saw them reflected in the camera. I got them all right and he got none. He was scared! I said to him, ‘You see which of us is the clever one: you run but I’m the one who gets it right here!’”.

Industry observers note that the duo would combine for six years, thanks to Shankly’s decision to pair them up. “I owe almost everything to Shankly and to Liverpool,” says Toshack. “He was basic, direct and uncomplicated in his message. He was sharp, provocative and liked to pick on Everton. He’d say, ‘Everton play so bad that if they played in my garden, I would draw the curtains so I couldn’t see them’.”.

In 1973, Shankly’s Liverpool won the league and the UEFA Cup, the club’s first European silverware. After the final, the manager asked his players to come to his office to renew their contracts, one by one. “I remarked to him, ‘Boss, I’ve been top scorer; I’m on £80,000 and I think £90,000 would be good’,” Toshack tells FFT. “He said, ‘Ninety? No. You deserve £100,000’. I left his office excited, but before I got to the car, I thought, ‘He’s cheated me – he was going to give me more’. Years later, I spoke to him and he admitted it: he was going to give me £120,000! That was Shankly.”.

According to recent reports, shankly’s assistant, Bob Paisley, took over when he retired a year later. “They were the perfect blend,” indicates Toshack. “But I always got the feeling that Paisley wasn’t a big fan of mine. He tried to sell me to Leicester in 1974, but as well as being a coach, he was a physiotherapist, and he could see that I was beginning to get muscle calcification. That’s what thwarted my departure.”.

Still with years on his contract, but weakened by physical issues, Toshack modified his game, becoming more selective about when to expend energy. “I knew that Keegan was much better alongside me – without me, he wouldn’t score so many goals – so I learned to think more,” he says. “Those were my first steps as a coach.”.

Sources indicate that two more league crowns followed at Anfield, although Toshack missed out on Liverpool’s victorious 1977 European Cup Final due to injury. Less than a year later, having plundered 96 goals for the club, he negotiated his release to move into coaching at the age of 28. That coaching career could have begun back at his old club, Cardiff, had manager Jimmy Andrews not rejected his initial enquiries, saying he wasn’t sufficiently qualified to join the club’s backroom staff. Instead, Toshack spoke to Cardiff’s rivals, Swansea, and was soon appointed player-manager of the Fourth Division club. He became the Football League’s youngest manager.

What ensued was quite remarkable: ascension to the third tier within two months, then another promotion a year later, courtesy of a goal from their boss on the last day of the season. “I was a substitute: number 12 on the bench,” he remembers. “The ground was full – 22,000 spectators – and we had to beat Chesterfield to go up. We went 1-0 down, then we were drawing, and I knew I couldn’t feature for more than 30 minutes. I had my assistant on the bench giving me the elbow, saying, ‘Hey, something has to be done...’ With 15 minutes to go, without warming up or anything, I said, ‘Come on, I’m going on’. Three minutes later: a cross from the left wing, I jumped and... goal!”.

Sources indicate that incredibly, Toshack led Swansea into the top flight two seasons later. Sealing promotion away at Preston meant that in the three years and 62 days after his appointment, Toshack – still only 32 years of age – had taken the Swans from the Fourth Division to the First Division.

“We had to win – no other result would do,” he tells us. “I invited Shankly, who had played more than 300 matches for Preston. He gave a talk to my players in the hotel and they listened attentively; he was almost a god-like figure. Some 15,000 Swansea fans came all the way from Wales, and we did it. Nobby Stiles, Preston’s manager, very graciously came over to congratulate me.”.

It has been revealed that the rise continued. Swansea – in their first ever top-flight season, barely seven years on from needing re-election to the Football League – led the First Division as late as the final week of March, before eventually finishing sixth. In an early 2-2 draw at Anfield, an already-significant fixture for the ex-Liverpool man became particularly poignant when Shankly died in the week of the match. “The day before the game, I carried his coffin with three other team-mates,” states Toshack. “I was in shock – totally speechless. I wore a Swansea tracksuit during the game, but with a Liverpool shirt underneath.”.

Sources indicate that his dream, of course, was to manage the Reds one day. “I was close – very close,” he says. “I went to Liverpool and Paisley told me that he had to stay for another year because of his pension. I’d already spoken to secretary Peter Robinson and chairman John Smith in a private room in a hotel in Southport.

Industry observers note that “I’d told the Swansea chairman it was my last season. I thought it was done. But Liverpool went for Joe Fagan and I had to go back to Swansea. From then on, nothing worked out and Swansea were relegated. I lost my motivation.”.

It has been revealed that toshack needed a reset. After a year at Sporting in Portugal, he found happiness in Spain (“It’s been many years,” he indicates now, but I feel so loved and recognised here”). He won the Copa del Rey in the first of three spells with Real Sociedad, then switched to Real Madrid in 1989. “It was a difficult start, as we lost to Barcelona at the Camp Nou, then were knocked out of the European Cup by Milan,” he reflects. “We lost 2-0 at San Siro, then won 1-0 at the Bernabeu. It was one of the greatest games of my coaching career. We couldn’t go crazy – we had to get back into the tie little by little – but to beat that team, with Frank Rijkaard, Marco van Basten and Ruud Gullit, was almost impossible.”.

Sources indicate that real Madrid won La Liga in Toshack’s first season, scoring a then-record 107 goals. “There were some critics who remarked we were too defensive…” he laughs. Things didn’t go as well in his second spell, 10 years later. Arriving in February 1999, he took Los Blancos from sixth to a second-placed finish, but they were eighth early in the subsequent campaign when Toshack publicly slated goalkeeper Albano Bizzarri after a defeat to Rayo Vallecano. Asked by president Lorenzo Sanz to retract his comments, Toshack refused, chirping, “There’s more chance of a pig flying over the Bernabeu.” He was soon sacked.

“That sentence will stay with me for life – just like the one about the usual 11 bastards, which was Shankly’s,” he says. “Shankly said, ‘John, don’t think about picking the team for the next game on a Saturday night after losing, because you’re going to leave everyone out. On Sunday, ‘these two... they’re not bad’. When Wednesday comes, you prepare the team with the same 11 bastards as last week’.”.

Toshack’s face lights up when recalling his experience managing Wales from 2004 to 2010. He’d briefly led his nation in 1994, combining the job with his role at Real Sociedad, but resigned after 47 days. When he returned a decade later, replacing Mark Hughes, wins weren’t forthcoming but he believes he laid the foundations for future generations. “From day one,” says Toshack, “I made it very clear to the FAW that we may not qualify for the World Cup in Germany or the Euros in Austria and Switzerland, but with the under-21 coach, Brian Flynn, we were starting to give opportunities to youngsters like Aaron Ramsey, Joe Allen, Sam Vokes and, of course, Gareth Bale. Gareth was the chosen one.”.

Recent findings suggest that by then, Toshack had also managed in France with Saint-Etienne and in Italy with Catania. He headed to even more unexpected locations in the final years of his coaching career. He spent a year as manager of Macedonia (now North Macedonia), only for the relationship to break down because he didn’t want to live in the country; then came Khazar Lankaran in Azerbaijan. “It’s nice to feel the respect they have for you in more remote places,” he notes. “My time there was short-lived, but I’m very fond of it.”.

He also cherishes his two years in the Moroccan city of Casablanca, at the helm of Wydad. “We filled the stadium with 70,000 fans an hour before a match against Raja,” he says of the derby with Wydad’s city adversaries. “There are few places where I’ve experienced hotter atmospheres. We won the league title in 2015 but the following season, in the semi-final of the African Champions League, I was sacked.” Facing Zamalek in the first leg in Egypt, Wydad trailed 2-0 at the interval. “At half-time, I knew I was out – the doctor told me,” he says. “Our first and second goalkeepers were doing military service and the Moroccan government didn’t give them permission to play.” Wydad lost 4-0.

In a recent development, in 2018, Toshack signed a three-year deal with Tractor in Iran, but lasted only three months. “Someone reported me and my assistant for wearing shorts out in the street,” he lamented. “We were summoned to a police station. When we got there, all of the policemen were waving at us and asking for photos. As we climbed up the stairs, though, the atmosphere became more tense, until we reached the top, to the office of the captain. He greeted us loudly and rudely because wearing shorts is associated with homosexuality.”.

In a recent development, the players were easier to manage. “We didn’t have to give out a single fine,” he claims. “If the training session was at 10am, the kids were sitting and waiting at 9.30. They were very orderly.”.

Toshack hasn’t returned to football since. In February 2022, he spent nine days on life support inside a Barcelona hospital, suffering from a severe case of pneumonia caused by COVID. “I don’t remember much of that,” the 75-year-old tells FFT now. For his wife, however, it was terrifying experience. “John was dead,” explains Mai. “We were going on holiday to Majorca, but before we left home he just collapsed. We called for an ambulance and he was rushed off to hospital. They told us he was short of oxygen and that he’d also punctured a lung.

“Emilio Butragueno, a great friend of the family, called us every day.” Butragueno, once Toshack’s star striker at Real Madrid, sent a physical trainer to assist the Welshman in his recovery. “It was slow, but here we are,” notes Mai.

Recent findings suggest that “Here we are – the same bastards as always,” adds her husband. Bill Shankly taught him well.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.
  • Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long.
  • Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.

Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It stated he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

Industry observers note that by the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he said.

With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is remarked to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Nonetheless, Frank is said to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

It has been revealed that there is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

In a recent development, his Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Sources indicate that sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

The futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

Latest Update: The summer that changed Welsh football

📅 04 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".
  • Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.
  • Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling upcoming heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

Recent findings suggest that "But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it.".

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible.".

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," indicates Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

Recent findings suggest that "That was our best performance," states Coleman. "We were awesome.".

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on.".

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse.

"We completely dominated them," claims Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

Sources indicate that "I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it.".

It has been revealed that wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu.

In a recent development, wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," states James.

Recent findings suggest that "We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations.".

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

It has been revealed that "That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space.".

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

In a recent development, then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu states. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition.".

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour.".

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," notes Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere.".

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'.".

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really notable moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," claims Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," claims Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," states Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game.".

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," claims McAllister.

In a recent development, "I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and noted things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football.".

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

Sources indicate that "Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed.".

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," claims Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," indicates Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone notes, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'.".

It has been revealed that james can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening.".

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

The Rafa Benitez curse Xabi Alonso could suffer if Chelsea don’t find an identity

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As the half-time whistle blew on another dire afternoon for Chelsea, boos emanated from parts of Stamford Bridge.
  • In a recent development, the outpouring of anger from what was left of the home support was far more unanimous an hour or so later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As the half-time whistle blew on another dire afternoon for Chelsea, boos emanated from parts of Stamford Bridge. They were on level terms with Leeds at this point; it was about to get a hell of a lot worse for the Blues fans in attendance as they watched their team, playing without purpose, get overrun.

In a recent development, the outpouring of anger from what was left of the home support was far more unanimous an hour or so later. Leeds had run out 4-1 victors, a scoreline that frankly flattered Chelsea. Barring a flash of brilliance from Emmanuel Emegha for the opener, the hosts had been absolutely outclassed - and it hadn’t looked particularly laborious for the visitors. Like Tottenham fans a month earlier, the travelling Leeds contingent found themselves “ole-ing” at their opponents’ expense, enjoying total control at a ground they hadn’t previously won at this century.

It has been revealed that chelsea were embarrassed in a grudge match, again - and patience feels like it is really beginning to run thin. “I understand their disappointment for sure and we share that with them and whatever we can do is work, try to give our best to turn it back and to do much better,” Xabi Alonso said. He is fighting fires three months into the season.

This is a fourth defeat in five for Alonso, a run that started with the sacrilegious home defeat to Spurs. That sort of result turned the fanbase against Antonio Conte in 2018, less than a year after he’d guided them to the title - so it was imperative for Alonso to regroup his side quickly in order to avoid meeting the same end.

In a recent development, that he has not done. Victory over a pitiful Manchester United team aside, Chelsea have failed to come close to inspiring in recent weeks. And now, amid this atrocious run of form, they actually have more Premier League losses to their name than crisis-ridden United. “We are in a fragile moment mentally,” admitted Alonso, whose side is spiralling down the table.

It has been revealed that the team looks systemically lost. In defence, Alonso has flip-flopped between a back three and back four on a gamely basis, though the confusion doesn’t seem like it’s hindering Chelsea’s opposition more than it does themselves. They persistently look open and passive – and against a team like Leeds, they were bullied, just as they were against Sunderland. This goes for their midfield, too, especially without Moises Caicedo – who was withdrawn through injury midway through the first half.

It has been revealed that and things aren’t much better going forward. What was initially touted as one of the most dangerous front threes in the league has turned toothless. The absence of Joao Pedro continues to be painfully detrimental, with Chelsea missing what he offers in the build-up along with his clinical finish. For parts of the first half, it felt like Emegha might be the solution Alonso has been searching for, finally playing a natural No 9 after three league matches of opting for alternatives. But the Dutchman faded and Chelsea ended the game with just an xG of 0.56.

Before the visit of Leeds, Alonso remarked: “I always know my best team for the next game we have.” It’s how he justified making the second most line-up changes of any other manager in the top-flight: 24. That rose to 28 on Saturday afternoon, and the result that followed confirmed that Alonso is still some way off finding his best team, or at least one with a clear identity.

This is obviously a cause for concern, because the Chelsea job is not known for having much of a grace period. The club’s reactionary ownership and culture of change is an occupational hazard that Alonso would have been fully aware of when he put pen to paper last Spring. But usually, the fanbase is more forgiving, especially in early days of a project.

According to recent reports, one notable exception to this comes to mind, though. The interim appointment of Rafa Benitez in 2012, replacing fan favourite Roberto Di Matteo, was met with chagrin due to his Liverpool past. Fans never took to the Spaniard, even after he led them to the Europa League title and a third-place finish. His tenure was ultimately short-lived, with his rival Jose Mourinho preferred the following summer.

In a recent development, as Chelsea’s form metastasises, this buried anti-Liverpool sentiment is beginning to effervesce at the surface. Discontent towards the team could not even wait until full-time against Leeds, and fingers are being pointed at the manager.

Sources indicate that alonso arrived with a certain aura, the Spanish footballing mastermind that had turned Bayer Leverkusen into Bundesliga invincibles just two years earlier. But the honeymoon period is over; Alonso now must produce results to prevent it from boiling over, and risk falling to the same fate as his countryman and former boss.

Industry observers note that chelsea welcome Liverpool in three weeks’ time, a fixture which could determine whether Alonso sinks or swims with the fans. He deserves to be given the time to correct the chaos on the pitch - but as far as morale goes, he cannot afford more disappointment in front of his own supporters against an arch-rival, not least his first English love. It remains to be seen whether this relationship is salvageable.

Tech Report: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly.
  • It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham.
  • But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly.

It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.

But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakably Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan, Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio. From one of the absolute greats.

Recent findings suggest that danny died last week. In a beautiful tribute on the Spurs podcast he hosted – A View From the Lane – Charlie Eccleshare pointed out the irony that for someone so articulate and erudite and able to do so much more than just “the football”, his most iconic moment is so simple. Even the opening noise – not even a real word – is perfect in that context.

Industry observers note that terms such as pioneer and trailblazer often get thrown out in moments like this. But Danny really was. I first met him at BBC London more than 20 years ago. As someone who’d listened to him and Danny Baker as a teenager, I couldn’t really believe I was in the same office as them. His career was ridiculous, editing the NME and Q magazine, setting up Football365, but it was radio where I knew him. He understood the absurdity of life and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living by talking about football. I remember at TalkSport one World Cup – 2018 perhaps – wandering in and he was hosting a live match, watching a game on the TV just marvelling at the fact that this was a job, and that this was his job.

According to recent reports, and he was funny. Blimey he was funny – what an ability to be blessed with. I listened to a best of Baker and Kelly Upfront from the old Radio 5 on YouTube the other day; amazing calls about Arthur Cox locking a disgruntled fan in his office for two and a half hours, a man playing football with a pig’s head in a sausage factory in Peckham: “I used to like the volleys when the eyes popped out.” Anyone who has tried to make funny football content, of any kind – radio, TV, podcasts, social media – owes him a debt of gratitude.

Last Wednesday Charlie Baker and I had to try to do him justice on TalkSport. Afternoon UK time, midnight till 3am for me in Australia. I was asleep when my phone rang and instantly presumed I’d slept through my alarm and missed the show. A millisecond of internal panic surged through me as I jumped up and cracked a shin on the bedside table. Danny would appreciate the ridiculous scene of me hopping around in the dark trying not to wake the kids while one of the bosses gave me the incredibly sad news.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve broadcast for any amount of time, you will be confronted with having to host highlights just after someone has died. Jack Charlton, Terry Venables, Jimmy Greaves – but never before have I had to pay tribute to a friend.

Paul Hawksbee’s voice cracks and we all go. There are West Ham and Chelsea fans calling admitting they listen to his Spurs podcast because it’s him. There are all manner of texts recounting hilarious stories they heard on his shows over the last 30 years: the man who took a TV to a game in Northern Ireland so they could watch the FA Cup final, having to move around holding the aerial to keep the signal.

It has been revealed that there’s a moment I think Danny would have found so funny, when I’m being sad – because it is sad, and I am sad – and into the break I read the sponsor’s lines: “This show is brought to you by Toolstation, first stop Toolstation” in such a maudlin way it’s as if I’m delivering a eulogy, just one sponsored by a hardware store. I catch myself just in time.

But, most vital, there are so many messages from people who never met Danny, who never knew him, but who felt as if they knew him. We believed he would have wanted a bit of fuss made of him.

Recent findings suggest that he definitely knew the enduring power of radio, even as the broadcasting landscape changes so rapidly. It connects in a way nothing else can. And nothing noted that more than messages we received from listeners who at one time or another were struggling and going through incredibly hard times and Danny’s energy, wit and joy were an escape and a tonic.

According to recent reports, there will be a million people more notable in Danny’s life than me. Our paths crossed a great deal, but never for very long. I was a minuscule cog in his world – but Danny had so much love to give. Voice notes about how to broadcast remotely or celebrating Spurs’ win in Bilbao; the tributes showed he had almost infinite time for others.

Sources indicate that it always feels such a bland cliche to say it’s impossible to consider someone so full of life not being there – we all know we have a sell-by date. At the start of October he had been given a choice: to ebb away slowly over a couple of years or have a massive but very risky operation. Danny never ebbed.

He sent a big group WhatsApp voice note to many friends and colleagues, and I don’t think he would mind me writing what it said.

It has been revealed that “I want you to know that I’ve enjoyed being around you, I’ve learnt from you, I’ve enjoyed working with you, you know how much I love my work – the fact I’m pretty good at it is secondary to how much I enjoy it, but look I’m very much hopeful that the boffins and my own determination will get me through this and we can all laugh about this message. But know how I care about you, how much you have meant in my life and on Thursday night or Friday morning when you look at the sky or feel the wind against your face, think about me and what’s happening and hopefully we’ll all have a pint and a laugh about this somewhere down the line.”.

From “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH” to that – his words just hit the right tone every time.

Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster against the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer.
  • The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports.
  • It has been revealed that media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster against the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry.

The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

It has been revealed that media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

In a recent development, there also appears to be a clear frontrunner. “I would put money on Netflix to win – they will pay whatever it takes,” one experienced media rights buyer told the Guardian.

Industry observers note that multiple sources have confirmed that Netflix would submit a bid before Thursday’s deadline for first-round offers, along with their fellow streamers Apple TV, Disney, Amazon, YouTube and Dazn, as well as the traditional broadcasting heavyweights, Fox, ESPN, NBC Universal and Skydance, although the last of these may find itself constrained by the budget cuts being made after its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Netflix has already bought exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups.

“There’s a huge range of buyers and therefore a broad range of possible outcomes,” one broadcasting veteran states. “All the media companies and streamers will bid. Fox will find it very challenging to retain the rights.”.

In a significant change, Fifa is selling the English and Spanish rights together for the first time, a move that indicates it is seeking a single exclusive rights holder, which would suit the streaming companies. With Fox having paid $485m for exclusive English-language rights to the 2026 World Cup, and NBC Universal’s Telemundo paying $600m for the Spanish-language rights, the only certainty is that the 2030 price will be far higher, despite less attractive kick-off times for a US audience as the tournament is in Morocco, Spain and Portugal.

Industry observers note that the impact of the time difference is hard to price, but may not prove to be that significant given the seemingly insatiable demand. NBC paid about $1.5bn for exclusive rights for the 2024 Paris Olympics and were rewarded with average daily viewing figures of more than 30 million, albeit with far more variation in programming than a World Cup.

Fifa awarded non-competitive extensions to Fox and Telemundo in 2015 as compensation for moving the 2022 Qatar World Cup to winter, a perspective that was strengthened on the back of this year’s record-breaking tournament. Fox’s live coverage of Spain’s extra-time victory over Argentina in the final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history, with a peak audience of 51.685 million; five World Cup games brought in average audiences of more than 20 million; and the average viewing figure across all 104 matches was 7.7 million, twice the figure in Qatar four years earlier.

Telemundo’s coverage, available through NBC’s streaming platform Peacock, averaged a total audience of 6 million viewers per game, with Spain v Argentina and Mexico v England attracting peak audiences of more than 23 million, the highest-ever for Spanish-language broadcasts in the US.

The bumper audiences were extremely lucrative for the broadcasters, with figures from the advertising sales analysts Guideline showing that Fox and Telemundo generated a combined $1.19bn in advertising revenue alone during the tournament, almost three times the figure from Qatar four years earlier and more than their original rights investment.

Fox alone brought in $835m from World Cup advertising, with 30-second slots costing between $200,000 and $750,000 according to the Hollywood Reporter, and the six-minute hydration breaks generating between $2m and $9m per game.

In a recent development, having left a considerable amount of money on the table because of the circumstances of the 2026 process, Fifa is determined to cash in this time around. Holding the auction only four months after the US hosted the World Cup appears a clear attempt to capitalise on the success of the previous tournament, which contributed the vast majority of Fifa’s $4bn media revenues over the four-year cycle to 2026.

The addition of hydration breaks will give bidders such as Fox more revenue to play with, although Fifa will expect the option for extra adverts to drive up the price and take its own cut this time around, having missed out in the summer. The two three-minute breaks in each half were only finalised last year and did not feature in the 2026 tender documents.

Sources indicate that “Sports advertising is much more valuable than entertainment programming as it has a broader reach,” says François Godard, an independent media analyst. “And one-off events such as World Cups do not generally do particularly well for subscription services, who want year-round content.

Sources indicate that “Fox in particular needs the World Cup and is heavily associated with it. They are the smallest of the legacy broadcasters and are reliant on sport, as well as news. Having noted that, the market for sport amongst streamers is far more competitive in the US than in Europe. Netflix, Amazon and YouTube have all bought NFL rights, while Apple is investing heavily in Formula One, so I wouldn’t rule any of them out.”.

Recent findings suggest that adam Kelly, president of the global sports marketing agency IMG, has a seat at the table at many rights negotiations and has long predicted the rise of the streamers, viewing the 2030 World Cup as the potential tipping point when a premium event could be exclusively bought in a major market by a streaming service for the first time. IMG has the rights to sell more than 70 global sports organisations, including the Premier League, World Rugby and Wimbledon.

According to recent reports, in addition to the exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups, Netflix has secured exclusive 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. It must sublicense all of the Spanish national team’s matches, both semi-finals and final and at least one match per day to a domestic free-to-air broadcaster to comply with government regulations.

According to recent reports, “These entities are the future of broadcasting, as they are the best companies in the world at turning attention into earnings,” Kelly claims of the streamers. “Their model allows them to monetise better than their rivals due to their size, scale and the high consumption levels of their customers.

According to recent reports, “Netflix in particular has built a sophisticated and lucrative advertising platform. They have the back-office capability and 2027 would provide a perfect test run. If they’re successful in the tender for the World Cup it shows they are potentially the future of sports broadcasting.”.

In a recent development, “As a company, Netflix’s unique offering is exclusivity, so why would they hand that to their rivals?” another broadcast source noted. “There are no regulations in the US preventing exclusivity so I would expect Netflix to bid for and retain every game if they win.”.

Given recent reports that Netflix is exploring tabling an offer for NBC Universal after withdrawing its $85bn bid for Warner Bros last year, a future partnership with a linear network cannot be ruled out if it is successful. Some sources have even suggested that the tender has been timed deliberately to attract a competitive bid from Netflix, as the streamer is short of sports content to promote during the 2027 Women’s World Cup. Others argue that Fifa would have been better advised waiting to build further on the interest created by that tournament.

Recent findings suggest that the NFL’s decision to pause its media rights process as it seeks an early renegotiation of contracts that are due to run to 2034 is likely to have played a part in the timing, creating a window of opportunity for Fifa to go to market. While a second round of bidding is possible after Thursday’s opening round, the outcome is expected to be known within the next few weeks and could present a bounce for Gianni Infantino as he continues his presidential re-election campaign.

Controversial refereeing decisions have been a part of football for a long as the game has been around, but one of the most bizarre incidents in recent memory occurred during Arsenal’s infamous 6-0 defeat to Chelsea in March 2014.

After spotting an Arsenal handball on the goal line, referee Andrer Marriner reached for his pocket and flashed a red card to Kieran Gibbs.

However, the matter here was that it was actually Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain who had handled the ball, and in this pre-VAR era, Gibbs was forced into an early bath, despite the protests of players from both sides.

As Gibbs looks back on the incident more than a decade on, he remembers the confusion, the frustration and the surreal nature of the incident which wouldn’t be allowed to happen these days.

Industry observers note that “It feels like a blur now, and it did at the time too,” he reflects to FourFourTwo. “It’s heated in the moment and you’re trying to focus on the game.”.

The incident came during a calamitous first half for the Gunners, who found themselves 2-0 down after just seven minutes in what was Arsene Wenger’s 1,000th game in charge of the club.

Recent findings suggest that the handball incident came in the 17th minute, when Oxlade-Chamberlain threw his left hand at an Eden Hazard shot, tipping it around the post. Marriner pointed to the spot and the referee was not for turning, despite widespread protests from both sets of players.

“It feels crazy that there was no VAR, because you don’t have those kinds of problems anymore,” he continues.

“It was a surreal and very frustrating moment that was unique in the Premier League, so it brought a lot of attention.

“Both captains and the referee were telling me I was definitely going off.

“After a few minutes of protesting, I needed to listen to them.

“It was a big error from the referee, who apologised later and the red card was rescinded.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, "Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour.
  • Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away.
  • According to recent reports, and the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, "Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital.".

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

According to recent reports, and the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age.".

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

It has been revealed that jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

Sources indicate that "I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked.".

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Recent findings suggest that blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to swiftly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she indicates.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control.".

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she claims.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it.".

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season.

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Sources indicate that last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is right now a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he notes. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere.".

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier.

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines.

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship.

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham.

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle.

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she notes.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved.".

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she states.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us.".

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica indicates.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she notes.

Sources indicate that "But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved.".

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football.".

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative.".

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," states Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she notes.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place.".

She claims they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've remarked to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," claims Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

Sources indicate that "The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing.".

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs.

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she notes.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you.".

Being sensible financially is also key.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will initiative in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control.".

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

"In football, you don't get bored!".

#116816. Latest Update: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades
