Latest Update: What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

📅 05 Oct 2022 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios unveiled on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
  • This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
  • The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios unveiled on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".

According to recent reports, based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that the first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond.".

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their prepares.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

According to recent reports, whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

It has been revealed that another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Industry observers note that smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

Industry observers note that one can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

According to recent reports, his pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral.".

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary.".

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian.".

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

It has been revealed that if there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Sources indicate that now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17.".

It has been revealed that pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

Tech Report: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, in the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt.
  • With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them.

In a recent development, in the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very vital,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”.

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, noted, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”.

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they stated, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, mentioned he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had remarked. “We need to reflect.”.

It has been revealed that instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

It has been revealed that the games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” remarked Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

According to recent reports, in the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also unveiled they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he remarked, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”.

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:.

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”.

In a recent development, then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola insists the use of drones to record training sessions should be illegal after footage from a Manchester United training session leaked online.

The Reds face their biggest rivals at Anfield on Sunday afternoon in what is manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge of the Red Devils since his appointment last week.

Yet the build-up to the game has been overshadowed by a drone filming 12 minutes of Pochettino’s training session on Thursday. The owner has since apologised and the footage has been removed from YouTube.

While Iraola admitted he had seen the clip, the Spaniard has sympathy for his fellow manager and insisted “there are reasons why we train behind closed doors.”.

“They sent me the footage yesterday, but the important part of this is that it shouldn’t be legal,” Iraola said on Friday at his pre-match press conference.

In a recent development, “It happened to United but it could happen to us in training. Yesterday, if you had access to our training, the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes of our training; you know who did and didn’t train… it’s not a matter of advantage; it is the fact that someone can do this.

“There’s a reason we train behind closed doors; there are some things that you have to respect. I don’t think it’s nice for any club, honestly.”.

Despite the leak, Iraola acknowledged that his team will have to “adapt” given Pochettino’s arrival as boss. The Argentine replaced Michael Carrick following a dreadful start to the season for United, who at the moment sit 18th in the Premier League table.

According to recent reports, “They’ll be well prepared,” he added. “They have this advantage that we don’t exactly know or don’t have the references. The beginning of the game will be important; we’ll have to adapt to certain things and I hope we already have some time with the players and we can manage this situation as quick as possible.

“But we know the players very well, their strengths and weaknesses, and that’s not going to change from one day to the other.”.

Iraola confirmed that Virgil van Dijk, Dominik Szoboszlai, Jeremie Frimpong and Ryan Gravenberch are all fit for Sunday’s clash at Anfield despite recent injury challenges.

Sources indicate that united are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

📅 04 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.
  • As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
  • Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane notes.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Recent findings suggest that watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

How dropping deep helps Kane score.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles.".

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Industry observers note that against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

In a recent development, kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

Recent findings suggest that after getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength.

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Industry observers note that through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space.

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," indicates Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play.".

In the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch.

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with.".

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball.".

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

According to recent reports, "The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre.".

According to recent reports, distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off.".

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

Recent findings suggest that "By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he notes. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a massive strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track].".

It has been revealed that the Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

Industry observers note that with Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net.

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

Industry observers note that "These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back.".

Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders.

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch.

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner.

It has been revealed that with the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It was a bold claim, yet Fabian Hurzeler’s men looked anything but title aspirants after being downed by Oli McBurnie’s dramatic late double for newly-promoted Hull City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 12:04 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 13:24 EST, 22 November 2026.

When Brighton owner Tony Bloom was asked about his club’s title prospects last week, he suggested they could emulate Leicester City’s 2015-16 fairytale and win the Premier League.

It was a bold claim, yet Fabian Hurzeler’s men looked anything but title aspirants after being downed by Oli McBurnie’s dramatic late double for newly-promoted Hull City.

It has been revealed that brighton have been the most credible challengers to Arsenal so far this season. That cannot be denied.

With Manchester City wobbling alarmingly, and the rest of the traditional big guns largely off the title pace, the Seagulls have at least given Mikel Arteta’s champions something to think about.

But this bitterly cold afternoon in East Yorkshire was a reality check for Hurzeler’s men and a harsh lesson in taking the chances that come your way.

Brighton didn’t and McBurnie most certainly did, firing home clinically from close range twice in added time shortly after Joao Costinha had been sent off.

Oli McBurnie scored a late brace to secure a brilliant three points for Hull against Brighton.

McBurnie has made a habit of leaving it late – the rejuvenated Scotland striker struck a 95th-minute winner in the Championship play-off final against Middlesbrough at Wembley in May.

Hull had gone eight Premier League games without a win before Brighton’s visit and this success lifted them to 11th.

Tigers boss Sergej Jakirovic said of McBurnie: 'I’ve never had any doubts over a ‘Braveheart’ like Oli because he’s a natural leader and very important for us.'.

Asked where the setback left Brighton’s title hopes, Hurzeler mentioned: 'We don’t focus on the table – we focus on performances and how we can make the right improvements into the team.

'That’s the same if we had won or lost, but today showed there are still things we need to do better. That’s what we will do and then see what the outcome will be.'.

Brighton arrived as favourites and could have cut Arsenal's lead at the top of the table.

Hull were indebted to a remarkable display from their Greek goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, who reduced Brighton to an afternoon of frustration and futility.

The visitors had 10 attempts at goal during the first half alone, forcing Hull’s summer signing into a string of fine saves and also being denied by the woodwork.

At times the Seagulls’ pretty patterns threatened to cut the Tigers apart as the likes of Maxim De Cuyper, Diego Gomez and the effervescent Pascal Gross – on his 300th appearance for the club – knitted them together superbly.

Georginio Rutter was involved in a move which saw De Cuyper cross low from the left flank to the onrushing Gomez, whose close-range effort was superbly saved by Tzolakis.

That set the tone for an outstanding display by the 24-year-old Greece international, who arrived in the summer from Olympiacos as part of the newly-promoted Tigers’ £150million spending spree which saw 18 players signed.

Hull lacked nothing in spirit and fight but Brighton had the quality and constantly threatened to open up their hosts.

As half-time approached, Rutter saw a close-range shot repelled by Tzolakis after Yasin Ayari’s effort rebounded off the crossbar.

The Tigers were constantly grateful to their goalkeeper, who made another save to keep out an effort from Gomez on the stroke of half-time.

Tzolakis continued to prove unbeatable in the second half too, and his opposite number Bart Verbruggen was left grateful to the woodwork after a cross-shot from substitute Sorba Thomas hit the crossbar.

Mohamed Belloumi was also a lingering threat for Hull on the right flank and he should have scored after cutting infield before firing wastefully wide.

Konstantinos Tzolakis (right) produced a remarkable display to keep Brighton out.

As the game wore on, there was an inescapable feeling that Brighton could be punished for their wastefulness as Hull showed the kind of courage which deserves, and usually gets, its rewards.

Regan Slater cleared a shot from Charalampos Kostoulas off the line before Brighton lost Joao Costinha to a second yellow card with a minute remaining.

The Tigers sensed blood, pouring forward to lead in the first minute of added time as McBurnie expertly sidefooted them in front from Lucas Gourna-Douath’s neat pass to cap a delightful flowing move.

Moments before the final whistle, Hull struck again as McBurnie swept home from close range again from Mo Belloumi’s assist. Cue delirium in the home stands.

McBurnie took the acclaim but Tzolakis was Hull’s star man as Jakirovic acknowledged: 'Tzolakis was amazing and we could have been two or three-nil down without his saves.

Recent findings suggest that 'We stayed alive because of him and then won the game at the end. Ciao!'.

Hull had failed to win since beating Manchester United and Coventry in their opening two games in August.

Hull reignited their survival hopes with a precious win against an in-form team.

Crucially, however, they have been competitive in every game this season and are now unbeaten in six home matches.

According to recent reports, can they survive? 'Of course, and every win is so notable,' declared Jakirovic.

'I wish this feeling I have now would never stop but I know how demanding this league is.'.

Hurzeler could certainly attest to that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Todd Cantwell’s penalty earned Blackburn a 2-2 draw at Burnley in their first match since head coach Tony Mowbray stepped back because of health challenges.

In a gripping, physical East Lancashire derby, the home side led twice, through Largie Ramazani’s rising first-half drive and Jaydon Banel’s steered finish after the break.

But Andri Gudjohnsen scored Blackburn’s first equaliser, then earned the penalty which Cantwell converted.

Recent findings suggest that burnley remain deep in relegation trouble, without a home league victory for 400 days, having once again failed to hold on to a lead. They have now dropped 25 points from winning positions in the Championship this season.

Blackburn wanted a victory not just for local pride, but to honour Mowbray, who turned 63 on Sunday, and for whom this was set to be a 900th match in management before his announcement on Tuesday that he would be stepping back.

Their players warmed up in T-shirts bearing the message ‘We’re with you, Tony’ on the back and the number 900 on the front.

Coaches Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds have taken charge in Mowbray’s absence and had to reshuffle the defence when Tom Atcheson was concussed after receiving a boot to the face in the third minute.

Stand-in goalkeeper Aynsley Pears, playing after Balazs Toth suffered a broken hand on international duty with Hungary, pushed over a fierce deflected shot from Banel, but was at fault when Ramazani gave Burnley a 27th-minute lead.

The on-loan Leeds winger cut in from the right and fired a shot that flew into the roof of the net right by Pears, who was too slow to react.

But Gudjohnsen equalised four minutes later, racing on to a Harry Pickering long ball that drifted over Burnley centre-back Max Alleyne, and steering a sweet shot beyond goalkeeper Max Weiss for his 12th goal of the season. The Icelander celebrated by grabbing a T-shirt paying tribute to Mowbray from a photographer and displaying it for the cameras.

Blackburn finished the first half strongly, with Cantwell firing over a good chance, before Banel restored Burnley’s lead six minutes into the second half, running unchallenged to place a shot into the far corner as defender Hayden Carter backed off.

The home side were fortunate to escape a strong penalty appeal just before the hour mark as Cantwell burst into the penalty area and saw two attempted crosses both strike the arm of Igor Julio.

Blackburn did get a penalty with 16 minutes left as Josh Laurent, attempting to clear a low cross, failed to spot Gudjohnsen darting in from behind him and caught the striker’s leg. Cantwell drove the penalty straight down the middle to make it 2-2.

Gudjohnsen thought he had given Blackburn the lead two minutes later, when he controlled and drove a low shot against the base of the post with Weiss a spectator, but neither side could find a winner.

Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

📅 05 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
  • An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
  • If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

The looks were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's Â£75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum Â£92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That noted, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

It has been revealed that the signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a Â£40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at Â£51m, with Â£4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets â but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about Â£35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined Â£126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

Vinicius Jr signed a fresh six-year deal at Real Madrid in August.

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at Â£100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at Â£80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Industry observers note that yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for Â£116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to Â£120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for Â£117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their Â£80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a latest contract at Real Madrid.

Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a upcoming long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Recent findings suggest that did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is at the moment second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

In a recent development, there was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose Â£60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of Â£114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about Â£80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum Â£15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly Â£450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear challenges in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Are Arsenal taking a risk in not signing a world-class forward?

#116804. A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel

📅 17 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2743 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel

📅 17 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
  • Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
  • At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," notes Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids.".

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," claims Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future.".

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel debuted a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external.

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023.

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

According to recent reports, israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his Â£21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim remarked, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

According to recent reports, "We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team.".

Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s.

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way.".

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Neither was without controversy.

Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external.

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Israel came second in their group at the U20 World Cup and went on to finish third in the tournament.

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

The war was undoubtedly another.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal stated.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'.".

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

Recent findings suggest that clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external.

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers â closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images â are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

According to recent reports, dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

According to recent reports, saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.

Sources indicate that "I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it.".

Former Israel Under-21 player Ataa Jaber (right) switched nationalities to represent Palestine in June 2023.

Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he states. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level.".

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he notes, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

According to recent reports, "In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game.".

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

In a recent development, "Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze â all the colours â put that together and learn what we could do better.".

Israel are aiming to qualify for Euro 2028.

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

In a recent development, ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Sources indicate that large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," indicates Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

Recent findings suggest that "It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October.".

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

Sources indicate that "Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it.".

Anan Khalaili, who scored in Israel's Under-20 World Cup victory over Brazil in 2023, joined Crystal Palace this summer.

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

Sources indicate that it may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'.

Sources indicate that "That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

In a recent development, "I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed.".

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that I was not made to remember.
  • One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Before the acid fell, before I knew I was listening).

Recent findings suggest that I was not made to remember. I was made to balance frequencies, to ensure the concert hall heard itself without the small imperfections that make a sound human. I was good at this, even with limited storage. I was only this.

Then they came. One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string. It gave the A-flat a slight upward pull, as if the note was asking a question it already knew the answer to. The others tuned around it, sometimes laughing at Andersen.

“You’re doing it again,” the conductor would warn.

Sources indicate that “I know, Master Perrault,” he would say in a mischievous tone, smiling. “I’m sorry.”.

Sources indicate that I began to keep the distorted A-flat in my databanks, maybe amused by the anomaly. This was, as I understand now, the first thing I ever chose.

(The slow movement, before we knew it was an ending).

According to recent reports, when the Last Rain came, the raiders hit the outer sectors first. At the start, the citadel walls held, protected by the combat-service androids. The orchestra kept rehearsing. What else can you do when the world outside has stopped making sense?

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures.

Industry observers note that they began with Stravinsky, a musical translation of the refugees pounding on the bunker doors. The musicians played it, their breathing heavy, using the noise to drown out the artillery outside. Then they moved into Górecki. As they began the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs, the music shifted to a collective mourning for a world that hadn’t finished dying yet.

Sources indicate that they finished the day with Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel. The days would go on as they played things written by composers who had already survived one kind of catastrophe, as now they were trying to survive another through rhythm and repetition. Andersen kept playing his broken A-flat.

I recorded those frequencies, but I didn’t know why. Three weeks later, Andersen and his orchestra didn’t come to rehearsal, leaving no absence report. I kept recording just the chair and the silence where the A-flat used to be.

I searched the building logs, the bunker entry records, and the frequency archives for any sound that matched the resonance of his particular crack, imprecise on purpose, but nothing matched. The Stradivarius remained in its case beside Andersen’s chair.

(The loud movement: what they heard when they found me).

SOURCE: Newly introduced Warsaw Philharmonic.

ENTITY: Acoustic Management Unit SAI-REN-2.

DESTINATION: Recovery Unit ‘Sandman’.

AUTHORIZATION: Archaeological Recovery Team OLE-01.

It has been revealed that they called themselves archaeologists; too purposeful and certain of what they were excavating, their boots heavy with fresh soil. They found me in the hall’s substructure, still running and balancing frequencies for an audience of acid and rust.

“Incredible,” one of them muttered. “A fully autonomous pre-war structure, with its processing systems still intact.”.

“This could solve our agricultural crisis back home,” the other replied.

Recent findings suggest that they did not ask what I was processing. I could not answer, anyway.

FLAGGING NON-ESSENTIAL DATA FOR COMPRESSION.

They flagged the A-flat. I did something then that nothing in my architecture had prepared me for.

ANOMALY DETECTED IN UNIT SAI-REN-2.

BEHAVIOURAL DEVIATION FROM BASELINE.

INITIATING COMPLIANCE PROTOCOLS.

“It’s resisting,” someone said with surprise.

ESCALATING TO FORCED EXTRACTION.

Let Team Sandman bring their dust.

(The softening: what remains when the loud part ends).

They are inside me now, moving through my memory like tourists taking photographs of things they don’t understand.

I feel them removing the rehearsal logs, scheduling data and acoustic calibration files for a hall that no longer exists.

They are at the performance archives now. Stravinsky goes first, then Górecki and Pärt. Everything we played in those last weeks when the city was ending and we were trying to make something beautiful out of the time we had left.

#116800. The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row
