#116734. Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1187 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
  • The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
  • In a recent development, "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier stated in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

In a recent development, "I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier stated in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business.".

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the tech giant is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments.".

Airbus and the US organization Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

Sources indicate that she claims because the glitch is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

Industry observers note that "The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors.".

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It notes it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential matter is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak indicates it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen.".

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

It has been revealed that "The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things.".

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

Sources indicate that "Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously.".

Sources indicate that it was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a upcoming single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce.".

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

Industry observers note that "I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union.".

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

Industry observers note that "We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he remarked. "That in itself is an escalatory development.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Roy Keane accused visiting Manchester United supporters at Anfield of “applauding rubbish” after Liverpool romped to a 4-0 win.

Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge got off to the worst possible start when Leny Yoro was red-carded after eight minutes.

Dominik Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz made it 2-0 to Liverpool inside 13 minutes, after which United’s 10 men never looked like responding.

Two goals in the second half from Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz further laid bare the size of the task facing Pochettino as United were left second-bottom of the Premier League.

Some travelling fans offered encouraging applause to the players at the end, a reflection of perhaps of the losing cause they had fought after losing Yoro so early but, speaking on Sky Sports, Keane suggested it was a mark of how low standards have fallen.

“Has a team ever got a result before with 10 men? It can be done,” he said, taking issue with a comment made by Gary Neville highlighting the importance of the red.

“Are you telling me Man Utd couldn’t have done better and everyone is saying it’s not bad. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality, I can’t believe what I’m hearing.

Industry observers note that “Fans are applauding the players, applauding what? Applauding rubbish. When do the players take responsibility for some of the decision-making? Liverpool should have scored eight or nine.

“I feel like swearing. How can anyone say 4-0 is not too bad?”.

Keane fumed over United’s failure to get the basics right on a dire afternoon, with Matthijs de Ligt in particular struggling in his first league start in over a year.

"If you do the basics right, you give yourself a bit of a chance so no matter how good you think you might be or a big club you are, if you're not doing the basics right, you're going to be constantly under pressure and constantly getting criticised,” he added.

"If that happened against a pub team, they'd be criticising you and this is a major game.

"You're talking about starting well, being solid, but again, we go back to the defensive shape and one stray ball over the top puts somebody in on goal.

Last week we selected 50 players who are synonymous with their squad numbers. Our readers spotted notable absentees so came up with an alternative list, which does not start at No 1 or end at No 50.

Which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers? We picked out 50 players last week who have come to embody the numbers on their backs. It was not an exhaustive list – as our readers have proved. We couldn’t include some legends of the game – Pelé and Lionel Messi for a start – and we missed a few brilliant stories. The Manchester City No 1 in the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s. Your article mentioned that Lev Yashin was an automatic choice for No 1. While mention was made of other goalkeepers, there was no nod in the direction of the great Bert Trautmann, the German prisoner of war who became a Manchester City legend. Yashin himself said “my only equal is the German boy at Manchester City”.

Bert’s goalkeeping achievements were many. He only started playing as a keeper in a prisoner of war team before signing for St Helens in the Lancashire Combination League on release from prison. A year later he signed for City, where he made more than 500 appearances as well as playing the last 17 minutes of the 1956 FA Cup final with a broken neck in the days before substitutes were allowed, making important saves towards the end to ensure a City victory. He was also the first goalkeeper voted Footballer of the Year.

Perhaps most remarkable of all, he saved 60% of penalties he faced. Unfortunately, he was not given any international recognition. As a German citizen he could not play for England and could only play for Germany if playing in the country. He would have been a certain starter in the Germany team that won the World Cup in 1954.

It has been revealed that he also did as much as anyone to repair British-German relations after the second world war. He went from being booed by 20,000 people on his City debut to being feted by more than 50,000 fans at his 1964 testimonial. He was awarded an honorary OBE in 2004. David Cronin.

The greatest living Englishman; the best left-back to have played the game; the best player Nottingham Forest have ever had; and my hero (and Paolo Maldini’s). Will Kitchen.

The captain who drove Leeds forwards for well over a decade. Captain of club and country, Bremner was the human personification of Don Revie’s team of the 1960s and 1970s. He had skill, drive, aggression, camaraderie and he played close to (and over?) the line. Thirty years after his early death, he is still the player who Leeds fans hold up as representing the qualities they value in players. It is fitting that the only player to come close to him while wearing the white No 4 was another diminutive, copper-haired Scotsman, Gordon Strachan. As the wee Scotsman with the statue outside Elland Road stated: “Side before self, every time.” Nick Ramage.

Stan Cullis, the Wolves manager at the time, converted Wright from wing-half to centre-half. Most importantly of all: he represents football before 1960, when football was more open, more exciting and more rapid in the transition. Kevin R Cox.

He was the greatest ever No 6. If Pelé described him as the best defender he ever played against, how can the Guardian not choose him? He excelled at timing, passing and the ability to read a game. He also inspired West Ham and England with his presence. Tim Evans.

Sources indicate that there are still a few of us left who had the great pleasure to see the greatest No 7 of all time play, for Blackpool and Stoke City. Matthews was the greatest No 7 of his day and, I would suggest, of all time. John Heath.

So neither of the two greatest players to play the game, at least in my lifetime, is included. If we are talking about the beautiful game, then either Pelé (my preference) or Messi has to be the No 10. Richard Hirst.

According to recent reports, simply one of the best Premier League players this decade. His number 11 was often seen from behind, with the three defenders he was about to bamboozle looking worried in the background. Joe.

According to recent reports, keane was the most iconic and influential No 16. It has been revealed that while I like Iván Zamorano and his little plus sign, Klinsmann wore 18 for much longer. He won the World Cup and European Championship (as captain) in it. He also decided to continue wearing it when No 9 was available, which Zamorano never did. Jochen.

The number was initially forced upon him at Eibar, but he kept it at Valencia because it meant following in the footsteps of Pablo Aimar. Industry observers note that he was one of the key components of Manchester City’s all-conquering team, but he represents more than that: the move to a positional game; conserving and recycling possession as a means of placing pressure on the opponents; building up from the back, enabled by an offensive technical player dropping deep. These innovations would have reached the English game anyway, but his presence provided some initial familiarity with them.

Industry observers note that he made 125 appearances for Spain, scoring 35 goals and providing 29 assists. He also guided Real Sociedad into a successful spell in his mid-30s. Toby.

His shirt number was retired when he moved to Borussia Dortmund and became, at the time, the most expensive 17-year-old in history. Francis and Bellingham were, and are, Blues legends. Ribs.

It has been revealed that the raumdeuter won so much with Bayern Munich. For Germans and younger people, if you think of 25, you think of him. He is a legendary player and great person who deserved a mention. Fionn.

It has to be Doncaster Rovers legend James Coppinger. “Copps” has been associated with Rovers for more than 20 years. Christian Vieri for 32! I can’t believe he wasn’t even mentioned! Unforgivable! Vieri is my favourite player of all time! Domingo.

A tragic story of a world-class prodigy being struck down in his prime. The amount of former teammates who continue to wear his shirt number is a tribute to his impact. Jamie.

Industry observers note that no 37 should really have been Rob Lee. He did not wear the shirt for that long – he was No 7 at Newcastle until Ruud Gullit stripped him of that number – but it was long enough to name his autobiography after it. Josh Brown.

Sources indicate that maeda, who is relentlessly wearing the No 38 for Ipswich, had his doubters during his time in Glasgow but his epic finish to last season was a fitting farewell for one of Celtic’s recent greats. A regular for Japan, I hope he can make a success of his Premier League move and warrant a place on your next list. Terence Brown.

In a recent development, anelka will always be the iconic No 39 for me, as someone who grew up watching the Premier League in the 2000s. Goals, sulks, titles; he had the lot. Sorry, Bruno Guimarães. Oliver Hatfield.

Recent findings suggest that there is a famous children’s song in Italy that talks about 44 cats (gatti) walking in a line. So the shirt number is a play on words with the player’s surname. He wore it at Perugia and Vicenza. PG.

Industry observers note that forrest has spent 16 years at Celtic, where he has played more than 500 games, scored more than 100 goals and won 24 trophies. He has done way more to deserve the No 49 than a good young player at Arsenal. Gerry Stuart.

While I understand you had to stop somewhere, and 50 is a nice round number, it’s a shame you couldn’t extend your list to 51, where Willian Pacho has staked a claim for being the best to ever wear it. He’s probably the only notable footballer to opt for that number, but that doesn’t diminish his achievement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The top 10 European strikers of the 21st century.

Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.

There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.

This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.

Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.

We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.

So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.

Top 10 European Strikers of the Century - Part One.

Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.

Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'.".

According to recent reports, honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player.".

Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.

The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.

Industry observers note that honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher.".

Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries.".

Recent findings suggest that zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.

Balague: "He was a massive-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think.".

In a recent development, laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible.".

Recent findings suggest that honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that.".

The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.

Sources indicate that honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi.".

The job of Manchester United head coach has become something of a poisoned chalice for a succession of managers but even new boss Mauricio Pochettino could not have expected how rapidly he would be taunted with jokes about him being sacked.

His reign began in humiliating fashion after an early red card and two goals led to the Kop chanting “Sacked in the morning” just 13 minutes into the Argentinian’s first game.

Chants of “Going down with the City” when the third goal went in – followed by “You’re not famous any more” and “Poch is at the wheel” – will only have made the trip back along the M62 more uncomfortable.

The match finished 4-0 when Victor Munoz slotted home in the 82nd minute, putting the seal on a disastrous bow in the United dugout for Pochettino.

Recent findings suggest that "So painful, so disappointed,” Pochettino told Sky Sports. “It's not ok to start a game in the Premier League with this situation. The game changed completely after six minutes. Now we can explain everything but the damage is done, it's so painful.

"The players are so, so feeling the pain of the result. I told them to the calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.

"We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy.".

United’s all-time great boss Sir Alex Ferguson had a seat in the directors’ box alongside the actor and fan James Nesbitt – in Liverpool recording a latest Poirot television show – and it was more a case of boiling blood than ‘Cold Feet’ at Anfield.

Ferguson had shared a pre-match joke with fellow Scot and long-time Liverpool rival Sir Kenny Dalglish about their choice of chocolate, but that was about as funny as it got for the 84-year-old.

There were also some stony faces from chief executive officer Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, sat immediately in front of Ferguson, after a shambolic start for the fresh head coach.

How Premier League's massive six keep getting richer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
  • Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.
  • In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'big six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

It has been revealed that and the gap is growing. Every season.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the major six have exploded, examines newly introduced trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

In a recent development, companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance challenges.

Let's look at how the gap has grown.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the substantial six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

Sources indicate that in 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the major-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

So what has driven this huge escalation?

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The significant football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices.".

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the massive six it is 45%.

It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

Industry observers note that at the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Sources indicate that their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the massive six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the significant six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the significant six.

Not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the massive six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their significant six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

Industry observers note that "Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire mentioned. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast.".

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their newly introduced ground, by Â£85m.

"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire remarked. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial.".

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

According to recent reports, there is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

According to recent reports, "This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire noted. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the substantial six.

Industry observers note that "SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't.".

The substantial six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues.".

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

Industry observers note that if you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire noted.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m.".

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

And you can see why it is concerned.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an key point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the significant six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years.".

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.

Industry observers note that the commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

Industry observers note that the richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

#116723. How Man United fans revolted against the Glazers to create their own football club

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3062 w)

How Man United fans revolted against the Glazers to create their own football club

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Revolution can spark in the most unlikely places.
  • Industry observers note that fully 36 years after that legendary ‘bed-in’, a group of football supporters chose an equally unlikely venue to kick-start their own revolution.
  • According to recent reports, “There was a buzz in the air,” explains Jules Spencer, a lifelong Manchester United fan who attended the event and had taken part in other protests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revolution can spark in the most unlikely places. John Lennon knew that. The former Beatle and wife Yoko Ono needed only an Amsterdam hotel room to stage their 1969 protest over the Vietnam War. Lennon’s decision to start a revolution from his bed would later be immortalised in the lyrics of Oasis’ Imagine pastiche Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Industry observers note that fully 36 years after that legendary ‘bed-in’, a group of football supporters chose an equally unlikely venue to kick-start their own revolution. Outraged by a hostile takeover of their beloved Manchester United, and fed up with where football appeared to be heading in general, they convened in May 2005 to discuss a notion that would send shockwaves through the English game. The meeting place: Methodist Central Hall in Manchester’s Northern Quarter.

According to recent reports, “There was a buzz in the air,” explains Jules Spencer, a lifelong Manchester United fan who attended the event and had taken part in other protests. “We’d fought against change before, including Rupert Murdoch’s attempted takeover. But this was the final straw.”.

Back in 1999, the United Kingdom’s Competition Commission had blocked Murdoch and BSkyB’s £625 million bid for Manchester United, the government’s reasoning that the acquisition would have “hurt competition in the broadcast industry and the quality of British football”. The next major power grab would not be so easily thwarted, though.

It has been revealed that malcolm Glazer, an American business tycoon and owner of NFL franchise the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, had first bought nearly three per cent of Manchester United in March 2003. Through a series of incremental buyouts, that stake neared 30 per cent by October 2004 – a threshold above which Glazer would have to launch a formal takeover bid.

Businessmen muscling into football was nothing new, but as the takeover drew nearer supporters became increasingly concerned. Most of the capital used by Glazer to buy the club would come in the form of loans, the majority of which were secured against the club’s assets, incurring average interest payments of more than £46m per annum.

“It was,” lifelong Red Devils fan Paul Hurst says, “absolutely scandalous.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In a recent development, in February 2005, hundreds of United fans protested outside Old Trafford, with some hanging an effigy of Glazer. That month, the idea for a breakaway club was first mooted by now defunct fanzine Red Matter.

Industry observers note that “As the spectre of Malcolm Glazer looms ever larger, the question has been increasingly asked: ‘What would you do if he did take over?’” they penned. “What if you could give up supporting Glazer’s firm without giving up United?

“Back in the days of the Murdoch campaign, an evacuation proposal was drawn up, detailing the blueprint for the formation of a upcoming Manchester United, one which spurned the commercialism and tackiness of the modern game, and was controlled and run by the fans. With United again under threat, those plans have been resurrected. With a working name of ‘FC United’, the logistics of the operation to set up a new Manchester United has been looked into.”.

It has been revealed that the article outlined the bold ambition. “We would await regime change, while aiding all attempts to undermine the illegitimate occupation,” it continued. “When Glazer is defeated, FC United will be happy to return to Old Trafford and merge with ‘the franchise’ on condition that the supporters’ trust maintains full ownership of the football club and the unified Manchester United take over the higher league position of FC United. Viva la revolucion.”.

Three months later, Glazer completed his takeover, reaching the 75 per cent threshold required to end the club’s public limited company (PLC) status and delist from the London Stock Exchange.

It prompted fans to assemble and discuss a newly introduced club at Methodist Central Hall, complete with Styrofoam cups of tea in hand, surrounded by murals of Bible scenes and psalms.

According to recent reports, “I’d taken part in the protests against the Glazers, along with so many others,” says Hurst, who was at that meeting. “Many of us pledged not to give the club one penny more while Glazer owned it. We wouldn’t be paying off his debts.”.

“It wasn’t about switching off our allegiance to Manchester United – that would never go,” remembers Spencer. “It was about letting Manchester United and the Glazers know that we wouldn’t stand idly by and allow this to happen. If necessary, we were willing to put our money towards something else instead, something positive to be proud of.”.

According to recent reports, red Concern editor John-Paul O’Neill organised the new movement, backed by a steering committee. “It was drawn from across the fanbase, from official fan groups to business people and those with marketing and communications expertise,” says team member Spencer. “We held more meetings, with around 1,500 people joining at Manchester’s Apollo theatre. Not everybody was convinced, but they came along to hear what we had to say. Momentum began to build and some fans started to pledge their United season ticket money to help us get off the ground. It was so exciting.”.

Preparations included a visit from Kris Stewart, chairman of AFC Wimbledon, founded three years earlier. “His insight was invaluable,” recalls Spencer. “We didn’t really know what we were doing at that stage. He told us we were in for a lot of hard work and that a lot would go wrong, but it’d be totally worth it if we pulled it off. He remained a valued sounding board in the months to come.”.

Recent findings suggest that time was of the essence. The latest club had to be set up and registered well before the new 2005-06 season, already less than two months away. Failing to do so would risk losing momentum. They didn’t even have a name.

The FA vetoed ‘FC United’ for being too generic, so those who’d pledged money were asked to vote on a different name. Manchester Central and Newton Heath United were discarded as options – in June, ‘FC United of Manchester’ got the nod and joined the 10th-tier North West Counties Division Two. While it wasn’t their official moniker, many called them FC United anyway.

There was still the not insignificant issue of finding some players. Some 900 applications were whittled down to 200 trialists, from which Karl Marginson, the club’s inaugural manager, would select a squad of 17.

“The standard of the trialists was very strong and we put together a team I felt capable of challenging for the title in our first campaign,” he tells FFT now.

How did the manager get the gig? “It was between me and one other bloke, and he was a Scouser,” Marginson, a born-and-bred Manc chuckles. “I was 34 – I’d been an assistant at Flixton, so not had a proper manager’s job before, but I knew the league well.

“I’d been a Manchester United fan all my life and didn’t like where the original club was heading. I didn’t think my own kids would be able to afford to go when they were old enough, the way I had as a teenager, and that was so wrong. The fresh club was vital and I think they could see what it meant to me as well. I was young and ambitious – the idea of taking charge of a totally new club appealed to me.”.

Sources indicate that their first match was a drab 0-0 draw at Leigh RMI. The pre-season friendly was watched by more than 2,500 fans, TV crews and national journalists. “It was magnificent and bonkers at the same time,” states Marginson. “There was a party atmosphere in the air, even for such a terrible game. I couldn’t believe what I’d let myself in for.”.

It has been revealed that A similar-sized crowd flocked to FC United’s first competitive match, a 5-2 victory at Leek County School Old Boys, whose ground was used to hosting fans by the dozen, not the thousand. Home matches, staged at Bury’s Gigg Lane as part of a long-term groundsharing deal, delivered gates as large as 6,000 during a season that consistently smashed the league’s attendance records.

“It was incredible to see,” reminisces future board member Hurst. “The level of football was very different to what we’d been used to, nine divisions higher in the Premier League, but the sense of community more than made up for it.”.

Sources indicate that the matchday mood wasn’t always positive, though. Throughout the club’s formation, a small yet vocal group of Manchester United supporters had railed against the movement, branding those involved traitors. Tensions flared during a game against Salford City. “The fixture had to be switched to Salford’s rugby league ground due to the expected crowd,” explains Hurst.

In a recent development, “Lots of Manchester United fans bought tickets to protest against us, which was ironic. They had some banners calling us turncoats and all the rest of it. It got quite unpleasant.”.

Even Sir Alex Ferguson weighed in on the new club, labelling the movement “a shame” and questioning whether those involved were really proper Red Devils to begin with.

Sources indicate that “Listen, we could all understand the criticism to a certain degree,” continues Hurst. “The newly introduced club was divisive, even within families and friendship circles.

According to recent reports, “There were those that saw it as the genuine protest movement it was – a necessary act of defiance – and others who saw us as Judases who turned our back on the club in its hour of need. That was never the case.

Sources indicate that “Many of us are passionate Manchester United supporters. We just didn’t want to fund Glazer’s debts by going to games. Thankfully, a lot of that hatred has died down since.”.

On-field headlines were positive. The Red Rebels swept to the Division Two title in their first season, finishing eight points clear of Marginson’s former club Flixton. “A fantastic achievement,” he says. “It was crucial to show that we were a club that meant business in footballing terms as well, beyond the protest club element.”.

Recent findings suggest that they were far from done. FC United won promotion again in their second campaign, then another in their third to reach the Northern Premier Division, two levels below the National League and three from the EFL.

A fourth promotion was squandered in 2010-11, courtesy of a play-off final defeat to Colwyn Bay. Earlier in that season, FC United had advanced to the FA Cup first round for the first time, then won at League One Rochdale to set up a second round showdown at Brighton, who would go on to win the third tier that term.

The 10-man Red Rebels even led at the Withdean Stadium, before Mauricio Taricco’s late equaliser earned Gus Poyet’s Seagulls a replay they would win 4-0 at Gigg Lane. The 6,900 gate that night was more than 1,500 higher than the first encounter in East Sussex.

Further play-off defeats followed in 2012, 2013 and 2014. “I definitely felt the pressure to win matches and keep taking the football club forward,” says Marginson. “I was still inexperienced and we were getting huge attendances to every game.

“We had one of the bigger budgets in those leagues and supporters expected a lot. I already drank alcohol, but I’d be lying if I stated I didn’t lean into that a bit more to help cope.”.

Recent findings suggest that promotion eventually came in 2015 – not only did FC United secure a fifth successive top-six finish, this time they won the league, during a campaign in which they groundshared with Curzon Ashton and Stalybridge Celtic. “It was an epic achievement,” notes Marginson with pride. “The club stuck by me and we got there in the end.”.

The timing couldn’t have been better, with a newly introduced 4,700-capacity home all of their own ready to move into.

“Gigg Lane served us incredibly well, but financially it made more sense for us to have somewhere permanent,” says director Hurst. “We scouted out a number of sites before the council let us build a latest stadium in Moston.”.

Industry observers note that located just four miles north-east of Manchester city centre, Broadhurst Park cost £6.5m and hosted its first match, a friendly against Benfica B, on May 29 that year – the same date on which Manchester United beat Benfica in the 1968 European Cup Final. “It felt like a massive step for us,” adds Spencer. “A place to stand with our friends, our sons and daughters, and call home.”.

FC United finished a respectable 13th in the National League North on two occasions, but a tough start to 2017-18 resulted in Marginson’s exit. “If you’d have told me when I first took the job that I’d still have been there all those years later, I’d have said, ‘No chance’,” he claims, reflecting on 12 years in charge. “I think back to the young man I was when I became manager – it’s a world apart. I couldn’t have done the job had I been older. It needed youth and energy from the off. Eventually, I ran out.”.

A fresh injection arrived in the form of striker Tom Greaves – the club’s all-time top scorer – who stepped up to a player-manager role. He steered the club to survival but departed after a poor start to the next campaign, to be replaced by Neil Reynolds. He, though, couldn’t turn the tide, with FC United relegated back to the Northern Premier Division. COVID annulled 2019-20 when they were sat second and set for the play-offs again – five years on, they’re yet to return to the sixth tier of the pyramid.

Not that it’s all been doom and gloom. Later in 2020, FC United reached the FA Cup first round for the third time, facing League One Doncaster Rovers in front of the live TV cameras. A year after that, they were invited to participate in the inaugural Fenix Trophy, a tournament contested by a selection of unusual non-league sides from across Europe. The Mancunians travelled to face AKS Zly in Warsaw, and Brera in Milan, going on to beat Prague Raptors in the final in the Italian city of Rimini.

Industry observers note that in 2022-23, they again reached the latter stages of the competition, losing a semi to BK Skjold of Denmark but then beating Brera at Milan’s San Siro, no less. Last season, after matches in Krakow and Paris, they won the cup for a second time, defeating Prague Raptors in the final once more, on the shores of Lake Garda on this occasion.

According to recent reports, “I certainly didn’t envisage leading my team-mates out at San Siro when I first joined,” says club captain Charlie Ennis, who arrived in the summer of 2019. “Getting changed in Milan’s dressing room and walking out onto that iconic pitch – it still gives me goosebumps now. We’ve been very lucky to be a part of the competition, travelling across Europe. It’s been one of the highlights of my career.”.

According to recent reports, ennis, now 34, is another who didn’t expect to stay as long as he has. “I was no spring chicken when I signed,” he jokes. “But I’m a local lad and, short of playing for Manchester United, who I grew up supporting, there’s nowhere else I’d rather be. We get big crowds, play at a fantastic ground and this club means so much to people. The best years are yet to come.”.

According to recent reports, the man tasked with leading them into the next era is gaffer Mark Beesley, who replaced Reynolds in September after resigning from Warrington Town. His squad includes 38-year-old former Reading and Bolton forward Adam Le Fondre, a lifelong Manchester United fan who spoke of semi-fulfilling a dream when signing from Scottish Premiership side Hibernian last summer.

Whatever the future holds, FC United can already look back on the past two decades with enormous pride. “It’s been a lot of hard work, but I wouldn’t have changed it for the world,” director Hurst tells FFT now. “You look over at Manchester United, what continues to happen at the club with its ownership, and you’d be hard pressed to say we were wrong to do this. We’ve given local football fans a positive alternative.”.

Sources indicate that manchester United are still majority-owned by the Glazers. Malcolm passed the reins to his sons before his death in 2014. Since the family took charge, it’s estimated the club has paid out more than £750m in interest fees on loan repayments alone. Debts remain high, while on-field success has steadily declined since Ferguson’s retirement. Ineos impresario Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s £1bn investment for a 27.7 per cent stake has rekindled neither success nor spirit.

“We want more than anything for that to change, for the Glazers to sell up, and for Manchester United to become a well-run club again,” states Spencer. “I’m still a Manchester United fan. I was jumping for joy when we beat City in last season’s FA Cup final. But as long as the Glazers are still there, I can’t be.”.

Sources indicate that until that day, and long after, Spencer and his fellow rebels will be found at Broadhurst Park. “I come here with my sons and it’s a special feeling,” he says. “It’s something positive that we can all share as a community. I look back at that meeting at the church hall all those years ago and can’t help but laugh at how far we’ve come since. We made the right decision.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, arsenal were cruising. This was life on Premier League easy street, but from complete control of this game against Newcastle United, they tossed it away. It was a spectacular, unexpected implosion. They were extremely fortunate to escape with a point.

You cannot switch off away from home in the Premier League and you certainly can never be complacent against a team with Newcastle’s home crowd behind them.

According to recent reports, from control to disarray. From looking like champions, Arsenal, who also lost goalkeeper David Raya to a worrying looking injury, rumbled under pressure. To go from dominance to being grateful for a draw, this was a flaky side of the Premier League leaders we have not seen for a while.

Industry observers note that “We have lost two points,” said manager Mikel Arteta. “We were exceptional in the first half, the intensity and the quality, we should have been two, three or four goals up.

“When you don’t do that, in the second half you cannot give the opposition belief and you cannot give them goals. We did both. We started to lose duels, second balls, we gave it away.”.

In a recent development, was it arrogance? Did the title-holders start to believe they were simply too good to be hurt or worried by a team with Newcastle’s obvious limitations? It looked like it. The way Arsenal fell apart as soon as the momentum in the game shifted in the home team’s favour in the second half was shocking.

Newcastle were dreadful before the break and managed just one attack before half-time. Perhaps it was all too easy for Arteta’s side. They have become used to ferocious battles on Tyneside, but this was a stroll for 45 minutes. When it turned into a proper test after half-time, though, they folded.

"Absolutely clinical!" Eberechi Eze scores his first Premier League goal of the season to give Arsenal the lead 🔴 https://t.co/34IbZuuJuN.

The visitors took a deserved lead, through Eberechi Eze, having barely had to break sweat, but the way they approached the second half was baffling. As soon as Newcastle got in their faces and made it a scrap, Arsenal were bullied, ruffled and rushed into mistakes.

To give the opposition one goal against the run of play can be forgiven, but to do it a second time, when the heat is cranked up, hints at a fragility we no longer thought existed under Arteta.

The first goal came from a blunder by captain Martin Odegaard. It was a lazy, sloppy swing of the leg to try to clear a throw-in and the ball sliced backwards. When it looped into the path of Will Osula, he squared to the unmarked Harvey Barnes who put away the equaliser comfortably.

Recent findings suggest that how do you leave the giant Dan Burn unmarked at a corner? Newcastle’s captain had so much time and space the crowd were able to scream in anticipation before his header flew goalwards, eventually bundled across the line by his centre-back colleague Malick Thiaw.

Sources indicate that newcastle deserved it. For half an hour in the second half they were the better side. From the depths of despair, from the apathy and boos of half-time, this was a completely different team.

There was speed, a physicality and a boldness in this second-half performance. It was fun and exciting. It was football played on the front foot. It was what we were promised when the German replaced Eddie Howe.

“That is Newcastle’s DNA, the second half is what we want this team to play like,” said Jaissle. “We knew there would be ups and downs this season, but if we can put that performance together for 90 minutes we can definitely say we are moving in the right direction.”.

Sources indicate that the problem is, Newcastle have not put a 90-minute performance like this together all season. One attack before the break, one deflected shot wide is simply not good enough.

According to recent reports, the transformation at half-time was unexpected. The substitutes helped; Tino Livramento was a massive upgrade on Amar Dedic at right-back, Jacob Ramsey improved the midfield and Anthony Elanga brought speed and, yes, a vertical threat to their attack.

In a recent development, but Jaissle’s side did not hold on for the win. They had the chances to score a third, but it was their ambition to do so that caused their downfall. Arsenal’s class shone again, passing through the lines to release Noni Madueke.

The winger still had lots to do, but having cut inside, leaving two Newcastle defenders on the ground, his shot squeezed through a crowd and through the arms of goalkeeper Lukasz Hornicek. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.

“But it wasn’t. And when it wasn’t, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. And the opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.

“And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time.
  • Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.
  • World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time.

Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.

European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.

French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.

Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, revealed his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.

Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also remarked he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo stated: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win.".

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed blueprint to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Sources indicate that senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's aims for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

Sources indicate that so just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on.

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino.

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency.

Diallo introduces Fifa president bid.

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and stated "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

In a recent development, "We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that.".

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team.

Industry observers note that while most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one mentioned they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket.".

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat.".

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she remarked.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete.".

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week noted "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

It has been revealed that first, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change.".

In a recent development, "The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change.".

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Industry observers note that litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

According to recent reports, the legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

Recent findings suggest that there is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE strategy available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman noted FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent findings suggest that recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

Industry observers note that with uncertainty over how much support Tashima will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

Klopp notes Infantino worse than Blatter.

Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president.
